intent: I am writing a survey on data-driven discovery of governing equations and I want to argue a single thesis: the practical limits of every discovery method trace back to two coupled problems -- (1) how it estimates the derivatives / closure terms that feed the regression under noise and data scarcity, and (2) what class of object it is actually able to identify (a closed-form symbolic PDE, a drift+diffusion SDE pair, a discrepancy/forcing term, or merely a black-box right-hand side). Across plain sparse-regression PDE discovery, PINN-plus-sparse-regression, Bayesian stochastic-DE discovery, SINDy-with-discrepancy/group-sparsity, and manifold-learning + random-projection approaches, I need to know concretely where each one breaks, what trick each uses to dodge the noisy-numerical-differentiation trap, and -- crucially -- what each fundamentally CANNOT recover even when it works. I also want the documented cases where the correct equation structure is found but the coefficients are wrong, or where the recovered model is non-unique.
nuggets: Rudy2017 (PDE-FIND) discovers a closed-form symbolic PDE by sparse regression (STRidge) on a library augmented with spatial derivatives, but its own Discussion flags the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky case as a limitation: the correct terms are identified yet the coefficients are badly underestimated under noise (true u u_x + u_xx + u_xxxx with unit coefficients, identified as ~0.46/0.48/0.49, ~52% error at 1% noise), which the authors attribute to error in numerical differentiation of the high-order derivatives -- i.e. correct STRUCTURE but wrong COEFFICIENTS.

Chen2020 (PiDL) attacks exactly that derivative bottleneck by letting a deep neural network approximate the solution and computing the library derivatives by automatic differentiation at machine precision (instead of finite differences / polynomial interpolation), coupled with l0 sparse regression via alternating direction optimization; it discovers the same canonical PDEs (incl. KS, Navier-Stokes, reaction-diffusion) from far scarcer and noisier data (e.g. ~1.95% of the Burgers data and 10% noise) where the authors state the SINDy/PDE-FIND family eventually fails on coarse, noisy KS data -- the direct head-to-head contrast with Rudy2017.

de2020 shows the deeper limit that none of the deterministic methods can dodge: applying SINDy to real falling-ball data does NOT recover the universal constant-gravity law, because unmodeled drag (a latent secondary mechanism) makes the data look Aristotelian (mass/density dependent); a universal physical law cannot be posited from data without simultaneously positing a DISCREPANCY model, and even after their group-sparsity fix the theory-vs-data mismatch persists due to subtleties in drag dynamics.

de2020's group-sparsity regularization (force every trajectory's model to select the SAME library terms) is the conceptual sibling of Rudy2017's disambiguation trick (use multiple time series at different initial amplitudes to tell the linear wave equation apart from KdV): both papers use multiple datasets/trajectories to suppress spurious terms and pin down structure -- group sparsity replaces naive SINDy's spurious height term with the correct gravity+linear-drag form across all balls.

Wang2022g (BISDE) is the only one that identifies a STOCHASTIC DE -- it recovers BOTH the drift AND the state-dependent diffusion term via sparse Bayesian learning on an Euler-Maruyama discretization, deliberately avoiding the data-hungry Kramers-Moyal / histogram-binning route that suffers the curse of dimensionality, and it beats the state-of-the-art SDE-SINDy (which failed to identify the model structure for all cases under limited data) on the same limited-data simulated systems.

Wang2022g documents a fundamental non-identifiability specific to the stochastic setting: two different SDEs can produce the same probability density function, so they share all statistical properties yet encode completely different mechanisms -- meaning even a perfect data-driven match of the PDF cannot guarantee the recovered mechanism is the true one (a 'what it cannot identify' caveat absent from the deterministic-PDE papers).

Galaris2022 differs from all the symbolic-regression papers in WHAT it identifies: it does not return a closed-form/parsimonious equation at all, but a BLACK-BOX right-hand side -- a trained shallow FNN or single-layer random-projection network (RPNN) -- after first using parsimonious Diffusion Maps with leave-one-out cross-validation to find the intrinsic manifold dimension and select coarse variables/features; it then does numerical bifurcation analysis (pseudo-arc-length continuation) on the learned surrogate, with the RPNN training ~20-30x faster than the FNN (about 8 minutes vs ~4 hours) at equivalent accuracy.
rationale: I read all five papers in full text on disk (Rudy2017 complete; Chen2020 lines 1-197 of 788 plus abstract/Table 1 covering all comparative claims; Wang2022g complete; de2020 lines 1-273 of 708 covering full methods/results-onset; Galaris2022 lines 1-639 covering full methodology + numerical results). No mismatched extracts -- every on-disk file matched its key's title/authors/abstract. Nugget 1: Rudy2017 DISCUSSION section (lines 90-99) explicitly gives the KS true vs identified coefficients (0.46/0.48/0.49) and Table 1 (line 84) gives the 52±1.4% noise error, attributed to numerical-differentiation error; the polynomial-interpolation derivative method and 'most challenging and critical task' framing are in Materials and Methods (lines 136-138). Nugget 2: Chen2020 abstract + RESULTS (line 35 automatic differentiation/l0/ADO; line 90 the 1.95% Burgers figure; line 97 'Existing methods (e.g. the family of SINDy methods) eventually fail in this case given very coarse and noisy measurements'; Table 1 line 65 gives 10% noise errors) -- direct contrast with Rudy2017. Nugget 3: de2020 abstract + Introduction (lines 14, 29-34) on the Aristotelian/constant-g failure and the need for a discrepancy model; Results (line 267-269) on persistent discrepancy from drag. Nugget 4: de2020 group-sparsity in 2.3.2 (lines 182-223) and Results (line 269) selecting gravity+linear-drag; Rudy2017 KdV-vs-wave disambiguation via multiple amplitudes (lines 61-71). Nugget 5: Wang2022g abstract + Methods 2.1-2.3 (drift Eq.9-19, diffusion Eq.20) and Results comparison (line 268: 'SDE_SINDy failed to identify the underlying model structures for all cases' under limited data); binning/curse-of-dimensionality at line 178. Nugget 6: Wang2022g Discussion (line 297): 'two different SDEs may produce the same PDF ... possess the same statistical properties but involve two completely different mechanisms.' Nugget 7: Galaris2022 abstract + Methodology (Diffusion Maps + LOOCV 2.1.1, FNN 2.2, RPNN/JL 2.3) and Numerical Results (line 602 ~1000 epochs/~4 hours FNN; line 606 ~8 minutes RPNN, '20 times faster'; line 35 '20 to 30 times'), and the fact that it learns the RHS as a black box (lines 50, 95, 178) rather than a closed form. All five are directly-answering because the question's two-axis thesis (derivative/closure handling AND identifiable-object class) genuinely requires each: Rudy=baseline symbolic-PDE+coefficient-failure, Chen=autodiff fix to that exact failure, Wang=stochastic drift+diffusion+PDF non-identifiability, de=discrepancy-model impossibility result+group sparsity, Galaris=black-box-RHS/manifold alternative. No off keys are listed because the prompt's five-paper thread requires all five as gold and provides no extra distractor keys; per instructions all gold_keys must come from the provided list, which I have honored.

intent: Across the modulation groups that reproduce the proton-to-helium ratio from PAMELA and AMS-02, I want to know whether the physical conclusion - that the time/rigidity behavior of p/He below a few GV is driven by the mass-to-charge ratio A/Z and by the different proton vs helium local interstellar spectra rather than by species-dependent diffusion - is robust to the numerical solver used (3D steady-state finite-difference ADI vs 3D/2D SDE pseudo-particle, with parameters set by grid-scan vs MCMC vs manual tuning). I also want the shared modeling assumption that the same diffusion/drift coefficients (same mean free paths in rigidity) apply to protons and helium, and where the groups note residual quantitative discrepancies.
nuggets: It is a shared assumption across these models that protons and helium share the SAME diffusion/drift coefficients (the same mean free paths as a function of rigidity), so one parameter set reproduces both species' spectra simultaneously (Ngobeni2020; Corti2018; Song2021).

Corti2018, using a 3D steady-state finite-difference ADI solver, concludes the dependence of the diffusion tensor on the particle mass-to-charge ratio A/Z is the MAIN cause of the time dependence of p/He below ~3 GV (Corti2018 abstract).

Ngobeni2020, using a 3D drift (finite-difference, steady-state) model fitting PAMELA p and He 2006-2009, concludes the p/He differences arise from the combined effect of A/Z and especially the DIFFERENT proton vs helium VLIS slopes, with p/He above ~3-4 GV settling near ~5.5 essentially independent of modulation conditions and thus revealing the VLIS shapes (Ngobeni2020).

Ngobeni2020 explicitly shows all mean free paths and the drift scale are independent of A/Z (A/Z enters only through beta = v/c in the rigidity-to-energy conversion), so there is no fundamental species-difference in modulation at a given rigidity - the p/He time/rigidity structure comes from beta(A/Z) and the VLIS (Ngobeni2020 section 2.1).

Song2021 (3D time-dependent SDE + MCMC) reproduces the long-term time dependence of the AMS-02/PAMELA p/He but finds the simulated ratio systematically LOWER than observed, attributing the residual to underestimation of the proton flux / the assumed proton LIS - a quantitative discrepancy that the steady-state groups also flag as LIS-sensitivity (Song2021 section 4.2).

All four groups specify the modulation boundary at the heliopause/termination shock (Song2021 heliopause 120 au; Corti2018 termination shock 80 au, heliopause 122 au; Ngobeni2020 heliopause 122 au; Wang2019 termination shock 100 au) where the LIS/VLIS is imposed as the boundary condition, and all use a Parker/Smith-Bieber-type HMF with K_perp ~= 0.02 K_parallel.

Wang2019 (2D time-dependent SolarProp SDE) shares modulation parameters across CR species (p, He, B, C) in the same period and derives their LIS by fitting Voyager-1 + PAMELA/BESS/ACE, reinforcing the cross-group view that one diffusion parameterization serves multiple nuclei and that the LIS is the key species-distinguishing input (Wang2019).
rationale: Read in full: Song2021, Wang2019; Corti2018 read methods+fit, Ngobeni2020 read methods+results incl. 3.3 p/He. Dunzlaff2015 and Zhao2013a OFF (methods/Markov papers without p/He A/Z study). Nugget 1 = Ngobeni2020 3.2 (same parameters, only A/Z and VLIS differ), Corti2018 abstract (same mean free paths), Song2021 4.2 (one parameter set for both). Nugget 2 = Corti2018 abstract (A/Z main cause of p/He time dependence below 3 GV). Nugget 3 = Ngobeni2020 abstract/3.3 (p/He ~5.5 above ~4 GV, VLIS-revealing). Nugget 4 = Ngobeni2020 2.1 (MFPs independent of A/Z; beta depends on A/Z). Nugget 5 = Song2021 4.2 (ratio systematically low, proton-flux/LIS underestimation). Nugget 6 = boundary positions Song2021 2.2 / Corti2018 3 / Ngobeni2020 2.1 / Wang2019 3; K_perp=0.02 K_parallel each. Nugget 7 = Wang2019 5 (shared params across species; LIS from Voyager-1 + PAMELA). Distribution spans 4 papers: A/Z+VLIS conclusion in two FD steady-state models tested under SDE+MCMC, with Wang2019 corroborating.

intent: I'm writing the methods-comparison section of a review on charge-sign-dependent solar modulation, and I want to pin down exactly how the competing modeling traditions parameterize the diffusion tensor versus the drift mechanism, and where they genuinely disagree. Specifically, I need to reconcile the full Parker-equation drift models (which write K_parallel, K_perp-r, K_perp-theta and an antisymmetric drift coefficient K_A or K_D separately, with weak-scattering versus rigidity-reduced drift) against the analytic force-field-style charge/rigidity-dependent potential approach, and understand what each says about how perpendicular diffusion competes with gradient/curvature drift to set the 22-year cycle. Where do these parameterizations make incompatible assumptions, and what do the numerical models claim the analytic potential cannot capture?
nuggets: The numerical drift models share a common diffusion-tensor parameterization in which the perpendicular coefficients are scaled to the parallel one: K_perp-r = a*K_parallel and K_perp-theta = b*K_parallel, with the polar coefficient enhanced over the radial one (Ferreira2000 uses a=0.05 and b up to 0.25 so K_perp-theta can be 3-8x K_perp-r; Nndanganeni2016 uses a=b=0.02 with a separate polar enhancement function F(theta) controlled by factor d, optimal d~5-7).

The antisymmetric drift coefficient in the weak-scattering limit is K_D = beta*R/(3B) (equivalently K_A); Nndanganeni2016 and Potgieter2021 both argue this weak-scattering value is too large at low rigidity and must be reduced by a factor f_D = (omega*tau)^2/(1+(omega*tau)^2), i.e. an explicit reduction multiplying by (P/P0')^2/(1+(P/P0')^2) with P0' = 1/sqrt(10) GV, motivated by Ulysses' observation of small latitudinal gradients.

Nndanganeni2016 distinguishes explicit drift reduction (modifying K_D or the HMF B) from implicit drift reduction (raising any diffusion coefficient, e.g. K_perp-r/K_parallel from 0.02 to 0.05 or enhancing K_perp-theta via d, which shrinks the intensity gradient nabla-f that multiplies the drift velocity), so drift effects can be suppressed without ever changing K_D itself.

Cholis2020 uses a fundamentally different, analytic charge/rigidity/time-dependent modulation potential Phi = phi0*(|B|/4nT) + phi1*H(-qA)*(|B|/4nT)*((1+(R/R0)^2)/(beta*(R/R0)^3))*(alpha/(pi/2))^4 rather than solving the Parker transport equation with an explicit diffusion tensor, and fits phi0 = 0.21-0.435 GV and phi1 = 1.15-1.95 GV (3 sigma).

The two traditions disagree on what an analytic/force-field approach can represent: Potgieter2021 states explicitly that the physics of the 11- and especially 22-year charge-sign-dependent cycle is NOT described by the force-field approach and that rudimentary force-field models can yield misleading anti-proton results, whereas Cholis2020 argues its augmented analytic potential reproduces charge-sign effects well enough to replace force-field models in cosmic-ray studies (excluding phi1=0 at ~16 sigma).

Both Torre2012 (2D Monte Carlo SDE) and the numerical drift models agree that the drift term is the ONLY charge-sign-sensitive part of the Parker equation, set by the product qA, so the sign of qA determines whether a species enters mainly via the equatorial heliospheric current sheet or via the poles; Torre2012 adopts rho_k = K_perp-r/K_parallel = 0.05 with a ~10x polar K_perp-theta enhancement, consistent with the Ferreira/Potgieter tensor scaling.

Potgieter2021 reports the perpendicular mean free paths lambda_perp-r = lambda_perp-theta are only about 2% of lambda_parallel at Earth, and that the drift scale lambda_D goes proportional to R at high rigidity but drops much more steeply below ~1 GV, the MFP-language counterpart of the rigidity-reduced K_D used in Nndanganeni2016.
rationale: Read in full (verbatim text on disk): Ferreira2000, Nndanganeni2016, Torre2012, Potgieter2021 (both pages, lines 1-227 then 228-end), Cholis2020. All five on-disk extracts match their stated titles/DOIs/abstracts; no mismatched extracts. Nugget 1: Ferreira2000 Eq (2) and Sec 3 give K_perp-r = a*K_parallel, K_perp-theta = b*K_parallel with a=0.05 and b=0.05/0.10/0.15/0.25, and Figs 8-9 give K_perp-theta = 3*K_perp-r and 8*K_perp-r; Nndanganeni2016 Eqs (12)-(15) give a=b=0.02 with F(theta) enhancement and the text states optimal d~5-7. Nugget 2: Nndanganeni2016 Eqs (2)-(4) give weak-scattering K_D = beta*P/3B and the modified f_D form with P0'=1/sqrt(10) GV; Potgieter2021 Eq (3) gives the identical K_D = beta*R/3B*(omega*tau)^2/(1+(omega*tau)^2) and both attribute the reduction to Ulysses latitudinal-gradient observations. Nugget 3: Nndanganeni2016 Sec 2 explicitly defines explicit vs implicit drift reduction and Sec 5.2 shows raising a from 0.02 to 0.05 makes drift effects nearly negligible at Earth. Nugget 4: Cholis2020 Eq (2) is the verbatim analytic potential and Sec III/Fig 4 give phi0=0.210-0.435 GV, phi1=1.15-1.95 GV at 3 sigma. Nugget 5: Potgieter2021 Sec 1 and 2.2 state the force-field approach does not describe the 22-year/charge-sign physics and is inadequate/misleading for anti-protons; Cholis2020 Conclusions recommend their analytic model as standard treatment replacing force-field and report excluding phi1=0 at ~16 sigma. Nugget 6: Torre2012 Sec 2.2 states drift is the only charge-sign-sensitive term set by qA, with rho_k=0.05 and a ~10x polar enhancement (Sec 2.1). Nugget 7: Potgieter2021 Sec 2.3 states lambda_perp-r=lambda_perp-theta ~2% of lambda_parallel and lambda_D proportional to R at high R with steeper drop below ~1 GV. Torre2012 is marked context because it confirms the qA-only and tensor-scaling picture but does not itself contrast the analytic vs numerical parameterizations. Synthesis is genuine: the diffusion-tensor scaling lives in Ferreira2000/Nndanganeni2016/Torre2012, the explicit/implicit drift-reduction physics in Nndanganeni2016/Potgieter2021, and the analytic-potential alternative plus the explicit disagreement over force-field adequacy spans Cholis2020 vs Potgieter2021 — no single paper covers it.

intent: For a paper interpreting AMS-02 and PAMELA lepton and anti-proton data, I need to assemble the quantitative picture of where charge-sign-dependent drift actually dominates the 22-year modulation versus where (anisotropic) perpendicular diffusion takes over, separately for electrons/positrons and for protons/anti-protons. Concretely: over what kinetic-energy window do drift effects peak and then vanish at low energy for leptons; how does the A>0 versus A<0 ordering of intensities flip with charge sign; and why do anti-protons behave 'awkwardly differently' from protons even though their drift physics is identical. I want the measured/modeled numbers and the competing diffusion-dominated versus drift-dominated explanations, including how the matter-antimatter ratios change over a cycle.
nuggets: For electrons, drift effects on modulation occupy a bounded energy window: Nndanganeni2016 finds the A>0/A<0 ratio deviates most strongly near ~100 MeV at Earth (smallest ratios ~0.28-0.35 around 50-100 MeV depending on drift strength), subsiding abruptly below ~10 MeV (diffusion takes over) and converging to unity above ~10-15 GeV; Ferreira2000 independently argues drifts become unimportant for electrons below ~100 MeV while perpendicular diffusion dominates there.

The charge-sign ordering reverses between species: for electrons (negative) in the inner heliosphere the A<0 intensity is HIGHER than A>0 (Ferreira2000, Nndanganeni2016), whereas for positive species the intensity for A>0 is higher than A<0 (Torre2012 finds qA<0 flux systematically lower than qA>0; Potgieter2021 finds positron A>0 intensity consistently higher than A<0); this is the qA-controlled drift signature.

Torre2012 attributes the AMS-01 versus PAMELA positron-fraction discrepancy below ~10 GeV to charge-sign drift, not new physics: during the A>0 period (AMS-01, 1998) the modulated positron fraction stays close to the interstellar ratio, while during A<0 (PAMELA, 2006-2008) the positron fraction is reduced below the interstellar value, increasingly so toward lower energy.

Potgieter2021 reports the anti-proton modulation is 'awkwardly different' from proton modulation despite identical drift physics, because the anti-proton VLIS has a peculiar spectral shape: positron modulation is diffusion-dominated at low rigidity (large, nearly rigidity-independent MFPs below ~0.4 GV) whereas anti-proton modulation is adiabatic-energy-loss-dominated at low rigidity as the MFPs shrink with decreasing rigidity.

Quantitative matter/antimatter ratio changes over the cycle: Potgieter2021 finds the proton-to-anti-proton ratio at 1-2 GeV may change by a factor ~1.5 over a solar cycle and the anti-proton intensity may drop by a factor ~2 at 100 MeV from solar minimum to maximum, and that the drift coefficient must be scaled to a very small value during the HMF polarity-reversal period to reproduce AMS-02.

Both lepton and anti-proton drift models predict a spectral cross-over of the A>0 and A<0 spectra: Potgieter2021 locates it between 1-2 GeV (above which A<0 exceeds A>0, opposite to the low-rigidity ordering); Nndanganeni2016 reports the analogous A>0/A<0 electron-spectrum cross-over around 1 GeV in the outer heliosphere.

Cholis2020 corroborates the drift-trajectory picture observationally from a negative-polarity (A<0) dataset: positively charged cosmic rays travel into the inner heliosphere along the heliospheric current sheet (~1 year, larger rigidity-dependent energy loss) while negatives reach Earth faster via the poles, and the charge-sign term phi1 is required at high significance (phi1=0 excluded at ~16 sigma), independently confirming charge-sign-dependent modulation seen in the lepton/anti-proton drift models.
rationale: All five papers read in full from on-disk extracts that match their titles/DOIs/abstracts; no mismatched extracts. Nugget 1: Nndanganeni2016 Discussion/Table 1 give max drift effect ~100 MeV at Earth, ratios at 100 MeV of 0.52 (d=7) and 0.28 (d=1) and ~0.35 around 50 MeV (Sec 5.1 weak-scattering case), subsiding below ~10 MeV and converging above ~10-15 GeV; Ferreira2000 abstract/Sec 2/conclusions state drifts negligible and perpendicular diffusion dominant below ~100 MeV for electrons. Nugget 2: Ferreira2000 Sec 3 (A<0 intensity higher than A>0 at 1 AU) and Nndanganeni2016 Sec 5.1 (A<0 spectra higher than A>0, characteristic of electron modulation in inner heliosphere); Torre2012 Sec 3.1 (qA<0 flux systematically lower than qA>0); Potgieter2021 Fig 9 text (positron A>0 consistently higher than A<0). Nugget 3: Torre2012 Sec 1/3.2/Conclusions tie the AMS-01 (A>0, positron fraction near interstellar) vs PAMELA (A<0, reduced positron fraction, larger at low energy) difference to drift. Nugget 4: Potgieter2021 Sec 5/6.1 explicitly call anti-proton modulation 'awkwardly different,' diffusion-dominated positrons vs adiabatic-dominated anti-protons at low rigidity (Fig 22 discussion, Sec 2.3 MFP slopes). Nugget 5: Potgieter2021 abstract and Conclusions give the factor-1.5 p/anti-p change at 1-2 GeV, factor-2 anti-proton drop at 100 MeV, and the requirement to make the drift coefficient very small during reversal (Sec 5.2). Nugget 6: Potgieter2021 Sec 4.2/5 note the 1-2 GeV A>0/A<0 spectral cross-over; Nndanganeni2016 Sec 5.1 cites the ~1 GeV cross-over (Reinecke and Potgieter 1994). Nugget 7: Cholis2020 Intro/Methodology/Conclusions describe positive particles along the HCS (~1 year) vs negatives via the poles during A<0, and exclude phi1=0 at ~16 sigma (Sec III). Ferreira2000 is context because it nails the electron drift/diffusion energy boundary but does not address anti-protons or the matter/antimatter ratios that anchor the question. Synthesis is genuine and distributed: the lepton energy window spans Ferreira2000/Nndanganeni2016, the positron-fraction anomaly is Torre2012, the anti-proton 'awkward' behavior and ratio numbers are Potgieter2021 only, and the independent observational charge-sign confirmation is Cholis2020.

intent: I'm building a heliospheric cosmic-ray modulation code and trying to decide whether to solve Parker's transport equation with stochastic differential equations (pseudo-particle/Markov solvers) or with a finite-difference grid scheme like ADI. I want to understand the concrete numerical trade-offs each group reports (stability, parallelism/cost, what part of phase space you get a solution at, dimensionality limits), and crucially whether groups fitting the SAME modern proton/helium spectra (PAMELA, AMS-02) with these different numerics end up recovering consistent diffusion-coefficient behavior and rigidity dependence. Pull from both the SDE-solver methodology papers and the application papers that fit spacecraft data.
nuggets: Parker's equation is traditionally solved by finite-difference schemes such as the Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method, whereas the SDE/pseudo-particle approach is the increasingly popular alternative (Dunzlaff2015; Corti2018; Song2021).

SDEs are unconditionally (numerically) stable while finite-difference/ADI schemes can become unstable for too-large time steps, and time-dependent 3D ADI is numerically unsuitable/unstable so that one spatial dimension must be sacrificed or the SDE approach adopted (Dunzlaff2015; Corti2018; Song2021).

An SDE/pseudo-particle solver computes the solution only at the phase-space point(s) of interest (a spectrum at Earth) and is embarrassingly parallel with independent trajectories, whereas a finite-difference solver computes f over the whole grid; the time-backward SDE formulation is the efficient choice for spectra at a point (Dunzlaff2015).

Corti2018 uses a 3D steady-state finite-difference (ADI) solver and, because a single model run is slow, fits AMS-02 monthly proton fluxes by generating a multi-million-model parameter grid (~3 million models, ~10 weeks, 4.6 TB) and interpolating, rather than a per-flux least-squares minimization (Corti2018 section 3).

Song2021 solves the SAME class of PAMELA/AMS-02 proton+helium spectra (2006-2017) with a time-dependent 3D SDE solver but searches the drift/diffusion parameter space with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, Metropolis-Hastings), achieving best-fit normalized chi^2 mostly < 1 (Song2021).

Multiple groups, despite different numerics, agree that the parallel diffusion coefficient magnitude (normalization K_0 and a double-power-law rigidity dependence with K_perp ~= 0.02 K_parallel) is anticorrelated with solar activity and must vary in time to reproduce the spectra (Song2021; Wang2019; Ngobeni2020; Corti2018).

There is a documented partial DISAGREEMENT in the inferred rigidity dependence: Song2021 (SDE+MCMC best-fit) finds the parallel-MFP rigidity slope can be STEEPER at low rigidity than high rigidity during moderate/minimum activity, contrary to the steepening-at-high-rigidity reported by steady-state ADI-style models, and Song2021 explicitly attributes such differences partly to steady-state-vs-time-dependent and ADI-vs-SDE numerics (Song2021 section 4.3).

Wang2019 solves Parker's equation with the SolarProp SDE Monte-Carlo code in 2D time-dependent form, fitting Voyager-1 + PAMELA to derive the LIS, and finds an empirical power-law DC ~ <B_E>^-n with n ~= 2 between the diffusion coefficient and the near-Earth HMF (Wang2019).
rationale: Read in full: Dunzlaff2015, Song2021, Wang2019; Corti2018 and Ngobeni2020 read through methods+results. Zhao2013a: ABSTRACT-ONLY - the on-disk extract is a MISMATCHED paper (DOI 10.1002/jgra.50235, an observation-based heavy-nuclei model that does not solve Parker's equation), so grounded only on the get_paper abstract and used as low-weight context. Nugget 1 = Dunzlaff2015 section 2 ('traditionally solved using finite-difference'), Corti2018/Song2021 echo ADI. Nugget 2 = Dunzlaff2015 2.2 (SDE unconditionally stable, FD not), Corti2018 (time-dependence makes ADI unsuitable), Song2021 (time-backward SDE unconditional stability). Nugget 3 = Dunzlaff2015 (solution at one phase-space point, independent trajectories, highly parallel). Nugget 4 = Corti2018 section 3 (3 million models, ten weeks, 4.6 TB, interpolated). Nugget 5 = Song2021 abstract/3 (Metropolis-Hastings MCMC, chi^2/dof < 1). Nugget 6 = Song2021 4.1 (K_0 increasing to 23-24 minimum), Eq.10 (K_perp=0.02 K_parallel); Ngobeni2020 2.1 two-power-law; Corti2018 2.2; Wang2019 4.4 (k_0 vs HMF). Nugget 7 = Song2021 4.3 (rigidity-slope difference; attributed to steady-state-vs-time-dependent and ADI-vs-SDE). Nugget 8 = Wang2019 (SolarProp SDE; DC ~ <B_E>^-2). DATA-INTEGRITY FLAG: Zhao2013a on-disk extract is a wrong/mismatched paper; re-ingest recommended; excluded from gold_keys.

intent: I'm trying to adjudicate the central debate over the sub-TeV cosmic-ray proton/nuclei spectral hardening: is the ~200-400 GV break an intrinsic source/injection effect, a Galactic propagation (diffusion-coefficient) effect, or partly an artifact of stitching together experiments whose absolute energy scales disagree? I want each camp's actual evidence laid side by side - the specific break rigidities different experiments report, the argument that ties the break to propagation rather than injection, and the explicit treatment of inter-experiment energy-scale offsets - so I can see which interpretation each paper's data actually supports.
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2011) directly observes a hardening in the proton spectrum at a break rigidity of 232 (+35/-30) GV, where the spectral index changes from ~2.85 (80-232 GV) to ~2.67 (>232 GV), with helium hardening at a similar rigidity (~243 GV).

AMS-02 places the proton hardening at a higher rigidity (~336 GV) than PAMELA's ~232 GV, and Lipari2019's global fit across PAMELA/AMS-02/calorimeters centers the hardening near ~650 GeV with a larger spectral-index step than the magnetic spectrometers alone indicate.

Schroer2021 argues the break at ~300 GV must be a propagation effect - a break in the Galactic diffusion coefficient (Rb ~290-300 GV in their D(R)) - NOT an injection/source effect, because the same break appears in secondary-to-primary ratios, which would not happen if the feature originated at the accelerators.

Adriani2011 (PAMELA) frames the hardening instead as a possible source effect, comparing to multi-source models (e.g. Zatsepin-Sokolskaya with novae/superbubble sources) and stating the data challenge the standard single-population SNR-acceleration-plus-diffusive-propagation paradigm (GALPROP does not reproduce the data).

The apparent disagreement in break rigidity and spectral indices between experiments is in large part a cross-calibration problem: Dembinski2017 shows each experiment's energy scale carries a ~10-20% systematic uncertainty that, for a spectral index ~2.7, produces ~18% apparent flux shifts, and derives explicit energy-scale offset/adjustment factors from a global fit.

Lipari2019 attributes the systematically softer slope above the break seen by AMS-02 (alpha2 ~2.72) versus the calorimeters (alpha2 ~2.44-2.62) to AMS-02's limited maximum rigidity (~1.2-1.8 TV) not capturing the full development of the hardening - i.e. a measurement-range/energy-scale effect, not a real spectral disagreement.

Lipari2019 explicitly enumerates that post-PAMELA models attribute the hardening to EITHER acceleration (two accelerator classes / two acceleration regimes) OR propagation (rigidity-dependent diffusion changing regime), leaving the source-vs-propagation question open.
rationale: Read in full: Adriani2011, Lipari2019, Schroer2021, Dembinski2017; Maurin2019 read in full but is the USINE propagation-code tool paper, does not adjudicate the break, so off. Nugget 1 = Adriani2011 (proton hardening 232 GV, 2.85->2.67; helium 243 GV). Nugget 2 = Lipari2019 Table 1 (AMS-02 break ~336 GV vs PAMELA 232 GV; combined Eb ~650 GeV). Nugget 3 = Schroer2021 Intro/section II (break ~300 GV must be transport not injection; appears in secondary/primary; Rb ~290-300 GV). Nugget 4 = Adriani2011 (Zatsepin-Sokolskaya multi-source, challenge paradigm, GALPROP fails). Nugget 5 = Dembinski2017 section 2 (10% offset -> 18% flux for alpha=2.7; 10-20% energy-scale uncertainty; GSF offsets). Nugget 6 = Lipari2019 (AMS-02 alpha2 ~2.716 vs calorimeters 2.44-2.62, attributed to max rigidity). Nugget 7 = Lipari2019 section 4 (acceleration-vs-propagation enumeration). Discrimination: source-claim, propagation-claim, energy-scale-artifact, and cross-experiment framing are in four different papers.

intent: I want to test how 'universal' the cosmic-ray spectral features really are across species and across the energy decades, and where the universality breaks down. Specifically: do protons, helium, and heavier nuclei share a common rigidity-dependent hardening/softening shape, or do they require different source spectra? Where does a single self-consistent transport model succeed, and what are the documented anomalies (the proton/helium index difference, the iron low-rigidity anomaly, the second softening, and the PeV-region experimental disagreements) that no single picture cleanly explains?
nuggets: PAMELA (Adriani2011) finds proton and helium have DIFFERENT spectral shapes/indices - the proton index (~2.82, 30-1000 GV) is steeper than helium (~2.73), a robust difference of Delta-gamma = gamma_p - gamma_He ~= 0.101 - already breaking the assumption of a single universal source spectrum for all species.

Schroer2021 independently concludes that protons, helium, and heavier nuclei require slightly DIFFERENT injection (source) spectra - H softer by ~0.05, He harder by ~0.02 relative to heavier nuclei - which is at odds with rigidity-only diffusive shock acceleration and corroborates the PAMELA p/He difference.

The hardening (and the higher-energy softening at ~10-20 TeV) appears to have an approximately 'universal' rigidity-dependent shape common to protons, helium and other primary nuclei, per Lipari2019, though the slope values differ between species - a universality that holds for the FEATURE shape even while the underlying source slopes differ.

Schroer2021 documents the iron anomaly: AMS-02 Fe is anomalously hard at R < ~100 GV and its Fe/O ratio is in tension with the standard transport model AND with HEAO/ACE-CRIS/Voyager data, a discrepancy (~30-40% near 1 GeV/n) that the authors cannot resolve and suspect may be experimental.

A single set of Galactic transport parameters (diffusion + advection, with a high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient) consistently fits intermediate and heavy nuclei (Ne, Mg, Si, S up to Fe except the iron low-rigidity anomaly) per Schroer2021, supporting the propagation-break interpretation for most species.

Semi-analytical propagation tools like USINE (Maurin2019) are the machinery used to fit this picture - solving the diffusion/advection transport equation for Z=1-30 nuclei with force-field solar modulation - and USINE was used to hint at the high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient from AMS-02 B/C data, the same propagation break invoked to explain the hardening.

Dembinski2017's data-driven global spline fit deliberately avoids assuming power-law-plus-cutoff component shapes and instead cross-calibrates experiment energy scales across 10 GeV to 10^11 GeV, showing the all-particle and per-element structure (the ~5 TeV dip, the knee at ~3 PeV) emerges from a world-average once energy scales are reconciled rather than from one source/propagation model.
rationale: Read in full: all five papers. Nugget 1 = Adriani2011 (gamma_p ~2.820, gamma_He ~2.732, Delta-gamma=0.101). Nugget 2 = Schroer2021 section IV.C/Conclusions (three slopes: proton ~0.05 softer, He ~0.02 harder; at odds with DSA). Nugget 3 = Lipari2019 section 4 (universal rigidity-dependent shape across species even if slopes differ). Nugget 4 = Schroer2021 abstract/IV.B (iron hard R<100 GV, Fe/O tension with model and HEAO/ACE-CRIS/Voyager, ~30-40% at 1 GeV/n, possibly experimental). Nugget 5 = Schroer2021 section III-IV (single transport set fits Ne/Mg/Si/S/Fe except iron). Nugget 6 = Maurin2019 (USINE Z=1-30, force-field, hints high-rigidity diffusion break from AMS-02 B/C). Nugget 7 = Dembinski2017 (GSF no power-law assumption; energy-scale cross-calibration; 5 TeV dip, 3 PeV knee emerge from world-average). Maurin2019/Dembinski2017 context (tool + framework) not direct adjudicators of species universality.

intent: What did the PAMELA satellite experiment actually find when it measured the cosmic-ray proton and helium spectra in rigidity, and why were those findings described as a challenge to the conventional picture of cosmic-ray acceleration in supernova remnants plus simple diffusive galactic propagation? I want the concrete spectral observations and the interpretation.
nuggets: PAMELA measured proton and helium spectra in the rigidity range ~1 GV to 1.2 TV (2006-2008 data)
Proton and helium have different spectral shapes / different spectral indices (the proton-to-helium flux ratio decreases smoothly with rigidity; proton index ~2.82, helium ~2.73, difference ~0.1)
Both spectra cannot be described by a single power law: the spectrum gradually softens around 30-230 GV and then shows an abrupt hardening at ~230-240 GV

These features (different p vs He slopes, and the breaks) challenge the standard paradigm of acceleration in supernova remnants followed by simple diffusive propagation, which predicts a single universal power law for all species
More complex / multiple-source acceleration and propagation processes are required to explain the observed spectral structures
rationale: Read Adriani2011 full text: abstract (line 30) and body lines 50-91 give the exact numbers - rigidity 1 GV-1.2 TV, gamma_p=2.820, gamma_He=2.732, Delta_gamma=0.101, softening 30-230 GV, hardening at 232/243 GV, single power law rejected at >=95% C.L., and lines 84-91 state it challenges the SNR+diffusive-propagation single-power-law paradigm (GALPROP fails). Single paper fully answers -> thin. Amato2017 (CR transport review) and MKachelriess2019 (CR models review) discuss these anomalies in general but are review context.

intent: I'm interested in using cosmic-ray antiprotons as a dark-matter probe. Using the precise AMS-02 antiproton data, what limits can be set on heavy (TeV-scale) dark matter annihilating into Standard Model final states, and is the thermal wino dark-matter scenario ruled in or out? Also how do these antiproton limits compare with gamma-ray limits from dwarf galaxies and the Galactic center?
nuggets: AMS-02 antiproton data are used to set 95% C.L. upper limits on the dark-matter annihilation cross section <sigma v> for all SM final-state channels, over DM masses ~200 GeV to 50 TeV

The analysis fits dark matter together with cosmic-ray propagation (GALPROP), using AMS-02 p, He and antiproton/proton data; secondary antiprotons alone fit the spectrum so no primary astrophysical antiproton component is required
The thermal wino (electroweak triplet) dark matter scenario is strongly disfavored / excluded by the antiproton limits, even with a conservative estimate of systematic uncertainties
For annihilation into quarks or gauge bosons the antiproton limits are significantly stronger than the gamma-ray limits from dwarf spheroidal galaxies
Cosmic-ray antiproton limits are more robust than Galactic-center gamma-ray/gamma-line limits, which depend sensitively on the (cuspy vs cored) DM density profile
rationale: Read Cuoco2017 full text: abstract (line 16) plus sections 2.1-2.4 (lines 30, 65-78, 105-119) give the mass range 200 GeV-50 TeV, all SM channels, the combined GALPROP fit, the result that the thermal wino is strongly disfavored even with conservative systematics, and the explicit comparison that antiproton limits beat dwarf-spheroidal limits for quark/gauge channels while being more robust than profile-dependent Galactic-center gamma-ray limits. Single paper answers fully -> thin. Potgieter2021 only motivates anti-nuclei as a DM test (context); not a quantitative DM-limit paper.

intent: What is the observational evidence from the Pierre Auger Observatory for anisotropy in the arrival directions of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, and which class of candidate sources gives the strongest correlation? I want the dataset size, the energy threshold, the significance, and the angular scale of the best-fitting model.
nuggets: The analysis uses 5514 Auger events above 20 EeV recorded before 30 April 2017, with zenith angles up to 80 degrees
A model based on starburst galaxies (SBGs, gamma-ray/radio-selected) fits the data better than isotropy with 4.0 sigma significance, with the maximum for events above 39 EeV
The best-fitting starburst model has an intermediate angular scale (search radius) of ~13 degrees and an anisotropic fraction of ~10% of events
A model based on gamma-ray active galactic nuclei (gamma-AGNs) is favored over isotropy at 2.7 sigma, best above 60 EeV, with a smaller ~7 degree angular scale
The anisotropy appears as an intermediate-scale excess (hotspot) of UHECRs, associated with the region around Centaurus A / nearby starburst galaxies

A maximum-likelihood ratio test against isotropy is used, with the two fit parameters being the anisotropic fraction and the angular search radius, and attenuation (GZK) of distant sources is accounted for
rationale: Read Aab2018 full text: abstract (line 9) and sections 2 & 4.2 (lines 33-37, 85-101 and the results table at 109-116) give 5514 events >20 EeV before 2017-04-30, starburst model 4.0 sigma above 39 EeV at 13 (+4/-3) degrees with 10+/-4% anisotropic fraction, gamma-AGN 2.7 sigma above 60 EeV at 7 degrees, the maximum-likelihood-ratio method, GZK attenuation handling, and the Centaurus A hotspot interpretation. Single paper answers fully -> thin. Batista2019 (UHECR open-questions review) and Mollerach2017 (high-energy CR review) mention anisotropy generally -> context.

intent: For numerically solving Parker's transport equation for charged-particle transport in the heliosphere, why would someone use stochastic differential equations instead of finite-difference schemes, and what does running them on a GPU buy you? Explain the time-backward pseudo-particle approach and any concrete performance numbers.
nuggets: Parker's transport equation is recast into an equivalent set of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) solved by integrating many pseudo-particle trajectories (Euler-Maruyama scheme, first-order accurate in the time step) and averaging

SDEs are unconditionally stable, unlike finite-difference schemes that can go unstable for too-large time steps, and they avoid a spatial grid / matrix inversions (e.g. those needed by ADI finite-difference solvers)

The time-backward formulation releases pseudo-particles from the observation point and propagates them to the heliopause boundary, which is far more efficient than time-forward (where most particles released at the boundary never reach the observation point and are wasted) when intensities are needed at only a few phase-space points
Because pseudo-particle trajectories are independent, the problem is embarrassingly parallel and maps well to GPUs (one thread per pseudo-particle), implemented with CUDA

Measured GPU-vs-CPU (OpenMP, 8 threads) speedups are roughly a factor of ~12 for one partition and ~32 for 720 partitions without fast-math, rising to ~26 and ~59 with fast-math; an order-of-magnitude (10-60x) overall improvement

A transition-probability solution is independent of the boundary function, so fluxes/spectra for different boundary conditions (e.g. a different local interstellar spectrum) can be computed without re-running, but changing diffusion/drift coefficients requires re-running
rationale: Read Dunzlaff2015 full text. Section 2 gives the SDE recasting and Euler-Maruyama; Section 2.2 lists the advantages (unconditional stability vs finite-difference, no grid, no matrix inversion vs ADI, boundary-independent transition probability); Fig.1/text justify time-backward efficiency (forward wastes particles); Section 4 + Fig.10 give the speedup numbers (11.8/32.5 no fast-math, 26/59.3 with fast-math; abstract says 10-60x). All nuggets verbatim from this single paper; it is the only slice paper deeply covering the SDE-on-GPU method.
